storyboard.claim: Humbert's respectable facade hides the monster; he exercises power over Dolores in the text itself.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Humbert pointing at Dolores in control — the mask icon signals a false public face hiding predation.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Continues from i159 about Humbert's facade fooling authorities; now shifts to his textual control over Dolores.
storyboard.addedInformation: Mask reads as false public face — literally what the narration describes (the monster underneath the European gentleman).

storyboard.claim: Humbert rarely records Dolores's voice — he silences her in his own prose.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Humbert talking while holding his book (the manuscript); Dolores beside him with no voice — he speaks, she cannot.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Specifies how the monster exercises power: by controlling what is recorded.
storyboard.addedInformation: Staging Humbert talking while Dolores stands silent makes the silencing visible — no icon reads as 'silenced.'

storyboard.claim: He quotes Dolores only in slang fragments he can mock — consuming her personality as thoroughly as her body.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Humbert holding notes (her quoted fragments) while Dolores stands diminished — he reduces her to scraps of slang.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Deepens i161's silencing: not just absent but actively mocked and consumed.
storyboard.addedInformation: Notes in his hand are the fragments he selects from her speech — the physical tool of reduction.

storyboard.claim: Dolores's actual voice is the agonizing silence of the novel — her reality is buried.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Dolores alone, slumped and sad — no icon, no one else, just her silence filling the frame.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: After two beats showing Humbert silencing her, the camera finally rests on Dolores alone with her silence.
storyboard.addedInformation: Isolating Dolores in the frame without Humbert makes the absence of her voice visible.

storyboard.claim: She stayed because she had nowhere else to go — that is the 'grand romance.'
storyboard.concreteVisual: Dolores standing on the highway with the chains icon — bound with nowhere to go, captive on the open road.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The devastating reason beneath the silence of i163: not love, captivity.
storyboard.addedInformation: Chains read as bound/imprisoned — literally what 'nowhere else to go' means. The highway set shows the irony: an open road that is actually a prison.

storyboard.claim: If we accept Humbert's framing, we ignore the real suffering of Dolores — committing the same crime as him.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Dolores slumped in pain, Humbert behind her turned away — the reader has been looking at him, not her.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Extends i164's captivity to the reader's complicity: we have been ignoring this girl.
storyboard.addedInformation: Putting Dolores first in cast and Humbert behind her reverses the visual hierarchy the novel has imposed.

storyboard.claim: Accepting the name 'Lolita' means accepting the world on Humbert's terms — it is the trap.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Humbert talking (naming her), the funnel-trap icon showing the reader being funneled into his framing.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The mechanism behind i165's complicity: the name itself is a trap.
storyboard.addedInformation: The funnel-trap icon reads as being lured in — exactly what 'the moment you accept the name' describes.

storyboard.claim: Humbert thinks he is the master manipulator, the brilliant director of this tragic play.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Humbert on a stage with the puppeteer icon — he sees himself as the one pulling all the strings.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Shifts from the reader-trap of i166 to Humbert's self-image as director — but he is not alone.
storyboard.addedInformation: Puppeteer reads as one person controlling others — literally what 'master manipulator pulling strings' means. The stage set reinforces 'director of this tragic play.'

storyboard.claim: Humbert is being shadowed by someone who exposes his true nature — Quilty enters.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Humbert walking on the highway, worried, with Quilty behind him — the shadow-self icon signals a dark double trailing him.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Undercuts i167's puppeteer: someone is behind him. The shadowSelf icon introduces Quilty as a double.
storyboard.addedInformation: ShadowSelf reads as a dark version of oneself — exactly what 'shadowed by someone who exposes his true nature' describes.

storyboard.claim: Quilty is the dark mirror of the novel — playwright, pornographer, shadowing Humbert across America.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Quilty in the foreground with the mirror icon, Humbert reflected — two versions of the same predator on the highway.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Reveals the shadower from i168: Quilty, introduced with his defining metaphor.
storyboard.addedInformation: Mirror reads as self-image/reflection — literally what 'dark mirror' means. Quilty first in cast establishes him as the new focus.

storyboard.claim: Quilty leaves taunting fake names in motel registers to drive Humbert insane.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Quilty smirking and holding notes (the guest register) — the game icon signals the cat-and-mouse play.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: First concrete action by Quilty after his introduction in i169: the register game.
storyboard.addedInformation: Game reads as a game — literally what the motel-register cat-and-mouse is. Quilty's happy expression shows he is enjoying the torment.

storyboard.claim: Quilty is playing a cat-and-mouse game, leaving names like Will Brown, Dolores Colo.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Quilty smirking and talking while Humbert stands behind him worried — the pursuer enjoying the chase.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Continues the register-game from i170 with specific examples; now names the dynamic directly.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: staging the two men together shows the dynamic but the specific pseudonyms are only in the audio.

storyboard.claim: Humbert presents Quilty to the jury as the true villain, pointing the finger to deflect blame.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Humbert pointing at Quilty in the courtroom — literally pointing the finger before the jury.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: After seeing Quilty's game (i170-171), now Humbert's counter-move: blame him before the reader-jury.
storyboard.addedInformation: Law icon reads as courtroom/legal — the narration literally says 'presents to us, the jury.' Humbert's point action matches 'points the finger.'

storyboard.claim: Humbert wants us to blame Quilty to absolve himself — the narration rejects this framing.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Humbert still pointing at Quilty in court — the struck-through callout shows the narration crossing out this accusation.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Directly rejects i172's finger-pointing: the narrator tells us this blame-shift is a lie.
storyboard.addedInformation: Strike style because the narration explicitly rejects Humbert's claim that Quilty is 'the bad guy' — it is a deflection.

storyboard.claim: Quilty is simply Humbert without the mask of literary genius — same predator, different packaging.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A sorter diagram with two buckets: 'Literary mask' (Humbert) and 'No mask' (Quilty) — the structural insight.
storyboard.onScreenText: Diagram labels: Literary mask / No mask
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The structural payoff of i168-173: not two villains, but one predator in two costumes.
storyboard.addedInformation: Sorter diagram shows the structural comparison the hosts make — same underlying nature, sorted by whether the prose disguise is on or off.

storyboard.claim: Humbert dresses up his abuse in Dante, Petrarch, and beautiful French phrases.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Humbert in a library holding a book — the literary references he uses as a costume for his crimes.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Expands the 'Literary mask' bucket from i174's diagram: what the mask is made of.
storyboard.addedInformation: Book icon reads as a literal book — and the beat is about Dante and Petrarch, actual books used as justification.

storyboard.claim: Humbert needs the aesthetic justification; Quilty just doesn't care.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Split frame: Humbert thinking/anxious on one side, Quilty idle and indifferent on the other — the contrast between needing justification and not.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The other side of i175: Humbert needs the literary disguise, Quilty operates without one.
storyboard.addedInformation: Split shot makes the contrast visual: worried thinker vs. unbothered predator.

storyboard.claim: Quilty represents the ugly truth of what Humbert actually is, stripped of the poetic disguise.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Quilty in the foreground as the shadow-self — what Humbert looks like without the prose.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Concludes the Humbert-Quilty comparison from i174-176: Quilty is the unmasked version.
storyboard.addedInformation: ShadowSelf reads as a dark version of oneself — literally what 'the ugly truth of what Humbert actually is' means.

storyboard.claim: The dynamic between Humbert and Quilty becomes clearest in the bizarre slapstick murder scene.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Humbert and Quilty entering a room together — the murder-scene setting established.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Transitions from the thematic analysis (i174-177) to its narrative proof: the murder.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: the callout names the scene; the staging introduces the location without spoiling the farce that follows.

storyboard.claim: Humbert tracks Quilty down to execute him, building it up as a Dostoevskian tragedy.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Humbert walking forward with purpose, worried intensity — the avenger approaching.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Inside the murder scene of i178: Humbert as the self-appointed executioner.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: the tragic self-image is in Humbert's head; only his tense walk shows it.

storyboard.claim: Humbert writes a dramatic death-sentence poem to read to Quilty before he kills him.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Humbert holding notes — the actual poem he wrote and plans to recite. Notes icon doubles the written document.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Deepens i179's tragic self-image: he has prepared a script for the execution.
storyboard.addedInformation: Notes reads as written text — and Humbert literally wrote a poem to read aloud.

storyboard.claim: Nabokov engineers the linguistic breakdown of the murder scene — the beautiful prose from page one starts to disintegrate.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Nabokov (the author) talking and holding the book — the architect explaining how he built the collapse of Humbert's prose.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Zooms out from Humbert's actions (i179-180) to Nabokov's authorial design.
storyboard.addedInformation: Nabokov is the subject: the hosts discuss the author's craft, not a character's action.

storyboard.claim: The hypnotic prose disintegrates into clumsy, fragmented sentences — reality descends into farce.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Humbert slumped and worried — his grand style collapsing around him, the eloquence gone.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The result of i181's technique: the prose the reader trusted since beat 1 breaks down.
storyboard.addedInformation: Humbert's slump and worry show the collapse physically — no icon reads as 'disintegration.'

storyboard.claim: Quilty is drunk or high, completely unintimidated — he treats Humbert with total indifference even when the gun appears.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Quilty idle and unbothered in the foreground, Humbert behind him — the supposed victim is not scared.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: After Humbert's collapse in i182, his target refuses to play the victim.
storyboard.addedInformation: Quilty's neutral/idle stance against Humbert's armed arrival makes the power reversal visible.

storyboard.claim: Quilty mocks the gun, then is forced to read the execution poem aloud — he treats the whole thing as absurd.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Quilty smirking and talking while holding the poem (notes) Humbert forced on him — mocking the executioner to his face.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Quilty's specific response to i183's confrontation: dismissive mockery.
storyboard.addedInformation: Quilty's happy expression is genuine amusement, not fake — he really finds Humbert ridiculous.

storyboard.claim: Quilty literally critiques the death-sentence poem while staring down the barrel of a loaded gun.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Quilty reading the notes (the poem) and talking — a literary critic at gunpoint, unbothered.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Escalates i184's mockery: not just dismissing the gun but editing the poem.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: the gun itself is not visible in the Antidote engine, but Quilty's calm posture conveys the absurdity.

storyboard.claim: Quilty chuckles at Humbert's poem, completely deflating his grandiose self-image.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Quilty laughing while Humbert stands deflated — the executioner humiliated by his victim's wit.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The punchline of i184-185's poem-reading: Quilty finds it funny, not frightening.
storyboard.addedInformation: Quilty's direct quote as the callout — his actual words carry more punch than a summary.

storyboard.claim: The gun jams and misfires — its physical impotence mirrors Humbert's moral impotence.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Humbert worried, holding something that fails him — his body language shows the pathetic futility.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: After Quilty's mockery (i184-186), the weapon itself betrays Humbert.
storyboard.addedInformation: Humbert alone in frame with his failure — no icon reads as 'misfire' or 'impotence.'

storyboard.claim: Bullets feebly drop from the sheepish muzzle — when he finally shoots Quilty, it is not a clean tragic death.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Humbert slumped and sad — the would-be tragic avenger reduced to pathetic fumbling.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Deepens i187's misfire with Humbert's own humiliating phrase.
storyboard.addedInformation: The narrator's own vivid phrase 'sheepish muzzle' is more devastating than any summary.

storyboard.claim: Quilty stumbles around complaining, wrestling Humbert in a messy brawl — the sheer absurdity demolishes Humbert.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Quilty reaching/wrestling with Humbert — two men in a clumsy struggle, no dignity, no tragedy.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The aftermath of i187-188's failed shooting: not a dramatic death but a wrestling match.
storyboard.addedInformation: Quilty first in cast because he drives the scene — his refusal to die tragically controls the tone.

storyboard.claim: He thinks he is acting in a Shakespearean tragedy, but Quilty forces him into a slapstick comedy.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Humbert slumped on stage — the grand tragic setting reveals the farce. Quilty beside him, unbothered.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The verdict on i178-189: the murder Humbert staged as tragedy played as farce.
storyboard.addedInformation: The stage set mirrors 'acting in a tragedy' but the callout names what it actually became.

storyboard.claim: He is not a tragic hero — he is pathetic, bumbling, and weak.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Humbert slumped and defeated — the struck-through 'TRAGIC HERO' rejects his self-image.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The explicit verdict of the murder sequence (i178-190): the narrator crosses out Humbert's self-cast role.
storyboard.addedInformation: Strike style because the narration says 'he's NOT a tragic hero' — the phrase is rejected, not affirmed.

storyboard.claim: After Quilty is dead, Humbert sits in his prison cell to finish his confession.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Humbert sitting in a room (prison cell), holding notes — writing the confession manuscript.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Shifts from the murder (i178-191) to the aftermath: the prison-cell confession.
storyboard.addedInformation: Notes icon reads as written text — literally the confession manuscript Humbert is finishing.

storyboard.claim: Humbert writes that he was despicable and brutal — appearing to express genuine remorse.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Humbert sitting sad with his notes — performing regret in the confession.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The content of i192's confession: his own self-condemning words.
storyboard.addedInformation: Humbert's own quoted words as callout — the viewer sees what the confession says before the hosts question its sincerity.

storyboard.claim: Even in his repentance he is unreliable — he is performing guilt for the jury, not feeling it.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Humbert sitting sad in the courtroom with the mask icon — his remorse is a performance, another false face.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Undercuts i193's apparent remorse: the sadness is a mask, not genuine feeling.
storyboard.addedInformation: Mask reads as false public face/pretending — exactly what 'performing guilt for the jury' means. The sad expression is the performance itself.

storyboard.claim: He wants credit for saying he is sorry — a gold star for realizing he was bad.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Humbert reaching out with a pleased expression — seeking approval from the jury for his apology. The happy face is not genuine joy but the smug satisfaction of expecting forgiveness.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Deepens i194's performance: the mask is not just for show but to extract a reward.
storyboard.addedInformation: The narrator's sarcastic phrase 'wants a cookie' captures the contempt. Happy expression is Humbert's expectant smile, not genuine happiness.

storyboard.claim: The hosts unpack the word 'my' in 'my Lolita' — one pronoun carries the novel's moral weight.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Humbert holding notes (the manuscript) with the magnifier icon — the hosts zoom in on a single possessive pronoun.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: After exposing the performance (i194-195), the hosts find the proof: one word that gives him away.
storyboard.addedInformation: Magnifier reads as close examination — literally what 'unpack the word my' means. The callout isolates the damning phrase.

storyboard.claim: The pronoun 'my' carries the entire moral weight — he still claims ownership over her even in confession.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Humbert pointing at Dolores with the chains icon — one word binds her to him, the possessive is a chain.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The verdict on i196's magnified word: 'my' is not a term of endearment but a chain of ownership.
storyboard.addedInformation: Chains read as bound/controlled — and the possessive pronoun is literally a claim of ownership that binds Dolores to Humbert.

storyboard.claim: Even admitting he deprived a child of her childhood, he still claims ownership — he never relinquishes his grip.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Humbert reaching toward Dolores — the grip that never lets go, even in confession.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Extends i197's chain metaphor into physical action: his hand still reaches for her.
storyboard.addedInformation: Reach action makes 'never relinquishes his grip' literal — he is still grasping.

storyboard.claim: He calls himself a monster but still demands his love was real and she belongs to him in art — the confession is the final prison.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Humbert holding the manuscript (notes) — the struck-through callout rejects his demand that his love was real.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The final beat of the confession sequence: even his last claim is rejected by the narration.
storyboard.addedInformation: Strike because the narration frames 'demands that his love was real' as the final manipulation — the hosts do not accept it.
